Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-20
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood CSM), Dana (MosaicHealth Platform), Rahul (Mosaic ML Infra), Lena (SRE), Michael (Head of AI)
---
Summary: Quick deep dive into Redwood Console request-tracing, error archaeology workflows, and how to run targeted replays against their dev dataset. Focus on: identifying model variant fallbacks, KV-cache misses, and stitching request logs to deployment traces.
Topics: tracing correlation IDs, request playback, prefix/KV cache behaviour, hosted vs private fallbacks, encryption/KMS, SOC2 audit logs, next steps for pilot.
Action items (captured live): see metadata section.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. uh quick intro, i'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account, with Priya our SE, and Marcus from success. you all seen the deck i dropped?
[00:12] Dana: yep we skimmed it, thanks. um we mostly want to understand how you'd actually, like, trace a request across models when we get degraded outputs. lately we've seen weird hallucinations on our triage assistant.
[00:25] Priya: cool, that's what we want to walk through. i'm going to share my screen — i'll show the request timeline, the trace graph, and then a live replay against a small sandbox. bear with me if the demo pops some weird metrics.
[00:37] Rahul: quick question before you start — we run mixtures of 13B quantized and 70B float on k8s. we also sometimes fallback to a smaller variant under load. how do you represent those fallbacks in traces?
[00:50] Priya: good question. our tracing includes model-variant metadata per segment. so in the trace graph the node will show model_id and quantization flag — eg redwood-gpt-13b-q8 and redwood-gpt-70b-fp16 — and you can hover to see latency buckets and KV-cache hit rate. sometimes the transcription will trim the names, sorry if the UI shows truncated labels.
[01:08] Lena: do you capture the reason for fallback — is it capacity, latency SLO breach, or explicit routing policy?
[01:15] Jordan: we capture policy decisions — the router emits an event: reason=fallback_capacity or reason=policy_cost_threshold. those are visible on the request span and you can filter requests by reason.
[01:24] Michael: our compliance person will also ask if those events go to audit logs. are those surfaced in the same console or do we pull them via api?
[01:32] Marcus: audit events are forwarded to the private control plane for Private customers; hosted accounts get an audit export you can push to S3. we'll attach the SOC2 appendix showing retention and schema.
[01:42] Priya: alright i'll start the replay — i'm loading a recent failing request id — note: the sample has redacted PII.
[01:48] [02:00] Priya (screen): ok here's the request timeline. top shows request meta, then steps: tokenization, runtime, model_inference, post_process. pay attention to KV-cache metrics — we show "kv_cache_hit_ratio" per step. this request has a near-zero hit ratio which explains the latency bump.
[02:20] Rahul: that could be on our side — we have a sticky session header that might change prefix and bust the cache. does Redwood cache by prefix hash only?
[02:30] Priya: we use canonicalized prefix hashing — but if your application injects ephemeral session data into prompts (like timestamps or ephemeral IDs) you'll see cache misses. we recommend a two-tier approach: client-side normalization + server-side prefix hints.
[02:45] Dana: hmm we do insert conversation metadata frequently. can you show the raw prompt and which tokens didn't match the cache?
[02:52] Priya: yep — in the request detail we show token-level diff markers and a best-effort guess at matched prefix length. it's not perfect — the ASR can mislabel tokens, sometimes it reports similar-sounding ones or splits contractions weird.
[03:05] [03:20] Jordan: also, in cases where the system fails a model and falls back we log the model_switch span. priya, can you show an example where the router chose a smaller model due to high queue length?
[03:33] Priya: (clicks) here's a trace where the latency SLO was 400ms and the in-queue time spiked; router selected redwood-gpt-6b as fallback. you'll see a model_switch span and a note that the quality_score dropped by ~12% vs baseline.
[03:50] Lena: how do you measure that quality score? is it automated eval or heuristics?
[03:56] Priya: it's a composite: historical logits divergence, rule-based checks (for safety), and customer-provided evals if you attach a golden set. defaults are heuristic but we can plug-in your prompt-level evals for pilot.
[04:10] Dana: okay can we search for all requests that hit a model_switch AND had safety flag triggered? we want to find patterns.
[04:17] Priya: yes — query builder supports boolean chain: model_switch:true AND safety_flag:true AND timestamp within range. you can also pivot by region or capacity_zone.
[04:27] Rahul: on the replay — is it deterministic? if we replay a request will you hit the same model variant or route fresh based on current capacity policy?
[04:36] Priya: by default replay uses the recorded routing decisions (an offline replay mode) so you see what happened. we also offer a live-resubmit mode to route under current policies for comparison. both are useful — replay for root cause, live-resubmit to validate mitigations.
[04:51] Michael: security — how are replays handled for PII? are logs redacted automatically?
[04:58] Marcus: we redact high-risk entities on ingest if you opt-in to redaction. otherwise we store encrypted payloads and provide redaction tooling in the console. for Private deployments we can configure retention and KMS.
[05:12] [05:30] Dana: can we map a specific user journey — say user-123 — across multiple requests and see which prompts mutated over time? our assistant sometimes starts with baseline and slowly drifts when context accumulates.
[05:42] Priya: yes — we have a session-joiner view where you provide session-id and we stitch all requests and responses, showing diffs. it highlights tokens introduced in each turn that likely caused drifts. we show a timeline heatmap of divergence.
[05:58] Rahul: interesting — does that capture any latent KV-cache warmup across turns?
[06:04] Priya: it surfaces a warmed prefix length per turn. you can see if the first turn warmed the cache and subsequent turns benefited. if you see repeated cache misses, that's a sign your prompt layout is busting the cache.
[06:15] Dana: in one failing flow our system falls back after the 7th turn — looks like a buildup. could that be memory pressure?
[06:23] Priya: yes, it could be model KV growth for long contexts. our runtime truncates or performs KV eviction under memory pressure; such events are logged as kv_eviction spans. you can tune the runtime eviction policy for dedicated pools.
[06:35] [06:50] Lena: from an ops perspective we need to ingest Redwood traces into our existing SRE stack (Grafana/Tempo). how do you integrate?
[06:58] Jordan: we export traces in OTLP/Jaeger format. you can stream to your telemetry backend or use our hosted observability with raw trace download. for Private customers we can enable direct OTLP endpoints.
[07:12] Rahul: latency vs cost tradeoff — can you show a per-route cost breakdown paired with latency percentiles? our CFO asks for per-feature unit economics.
[07:22] Priya: yes the Console has per-route charts showing cost_per_1k_tokens and p50/p90 latency and request_count; you can group by model_variant and by deployment_type (Hosted vs Dedicated). also Optimize suggestions will propose quantization and batching parameters with estimated savings.
[07:38] Dana: about quantization — we saw artifacts when moving to q4_0 on some edge prompts. can Redwood detect quality regressions after quantization changes?
[07:47] Priya: we do regression alerts — you can attach a test-prompt set and pin alert thresholds. when a rollout switches a model variant or quantization profile, we run canary evals and compare to baseline, alerting on metric drift.
[07:59] Michael: excellent. one more thing — on private deployment, how does key management work? we need HSM/KMS and audit trail for decryption events.
[08:08] Marcus: we support AWS KMS and bring-your-own HSM connectors for on-prem. decryption events are captured in the audit export with request-level context. we can show a sample schema.
[08:20] [08:40] Priya: switching back to the replay, i'm now toggling live-resubmit — you'll see the router choose a different variant because our demo cluster has different load. note response is slightly faster but quality shifted; that's the typical tradeoff.
[08:55] Rahul: for the pilot we want to run a 2-week replay run on our dev traffic and then a staged live resubmit against a canary. what's the recommended setup?
[09:05] Priya: recommended: 1) export a week of dev traffic with PII redaction; 2) run offline replay to compute error rate deltas and KV-cache stats; 3) apply Optimize suggestions (batching/quant profiles); 4) run a small live-resubmit A/B against 5% traffic in dedicated pool; 5) evaluate. we'll help with scripts.
[09:24] Dana: perfect. when you mention caching metrics, are those token-level or prompt-level? we sometimes need to attribute cost to specific prompt templates.
[09:34] Priya: we provide both token-level granularity and grouped by prompt-template if you pass a template_id or use our SDK to annotate requests. we add metadata tags which show up in the console pivot.
[09:45] [10:00] Lena: one of our worries: if we bring Redwood Private into our VPC, how do you handle upgrades and schema migrations for traces? we can't accept downtime.
[10:09] Jordan: Private's control plane supports zero-downtime rolling upgrades and trace schema compatibility modes. breaking schema changes are opt-in and we provide migration tooling. for less risk we recommend a staging private cluster for a week before prod cutover.
[10:25] Michael: okay let's walk through a concrete failure — we sent 3 request IDs before the call. Dana, do you have them handy?
[10:32] Dana: yes — IDs: mh-20250930-aaa12, mh-20251002-bb33, mh-20251015-ccc98. we attached them to the calendar invite — not sure if you pulled them.
[10:42] Priya: i have one loaded — mh-20250930-aaa12 — looking at the trace now. first span shows prompt normalization added a timestamp that caused cache miss; second span shows model_switch to 6b; third shows safety_rule flag and a post_process rewrite. the combination is likely the cause.
[10:58] Rahul: the timestamp insertion is from our side — a bug in the client lib. would you annotate where the timestamp appears?
[11:06] Priya: yes — i'll open the token diff view. see tokens [token_14..token_18] contain an ISO string — ASR split it across tokens. that breaks the prefix. again, tokenization mismatches are common source of misses.
[11:19] [11:35] Jordan: i want to highlight another capability — the request inspector can show correlated infra metrics (GPU mem, queue length). in this trace the GPU mem looks normal but queue length spiked to 90%. that aligns with fallback.
[11:48] Lena: fine, so mitigation path would be either change client to avoid timestamps, or we can warm the cache by injecting a stable prefix?
[11:57] Priya: either works. for pilot i recommend client normalization + create a prefix_warm job that issues synthetic warmup requests. Optimize can help generate warmup templates.
[12:08] Dana: about the warmup — will that cost us extra tokens? CFO might push back.
[12:14] Jordan: yes it has token cost but Optimize will estimate cost vs savings. sometimes small warmup jobs reduce downstream token usage by avoiding full context recomputation.
[12:25] Rahul: can we schedule a short benchmark to quantify delta? we'll need a CSV with baseline vs warmed run.
[12:31] Priya: i'll include a benchmark sheet in the artifacts. also the replay script outputs CSV summaries.
[12:38] [12:50] Marcus: i'm noting next steps: priya will upload replay script + README; jordan will send SOC2 + KMS notes; dana will provide 3 failing request IDs (done) and a representative prompt set; then we'll schedule pilot kickoff.
[13:03] Michael: curious — you mentioned canary evals on rollouts. can we plug in an automatic rollback if quality dips beyond threshold?
[13:12] Priya: yes — rollout policies can include automated rollback with a cooldown and a fallback model. you control thresholds and SLA windows.
[13:22] Lena: are there any limitations for longer context models — like with 128k contexts? we are considering a long-context route for particular documents.
[13:31] Priya: long contexts increase KV memory; our runtime supports segmented attention and chunked KV to maintain throughput, but you'll need Dedicated pools with larger GPUs. we can recommend instance types. also note cost escalates non-linearly with context length.
[13:47] Rahul: one more compliance nit — can the console redact or mask tokens in traces before they leave our VPC?
[13:55] Marcus: for Private, yes — we can enable in-line redaction and never export raw payloads. for Hosted we offer a managed redaction pipeline.
[14:05] [14:20] Dana: anything else we should be aware of when running the offline replay? durability, replay idempotency?
[14:28] Priya: replays are idempotent; we treat them as read-only unless you enable live-resubmit. they won't charge generation tokens unless you opt into live-resubmit. offline replays compute metrics locally. ensure you mark PII for redaction before upload.
[14:40] Jordan: quick commercial note — given your volume, a Dedicated pilot is the usual path. we'll propose pricing for a 3-month pilot with a commit level and an option to convert to Private.
[14:52] Michael: sounds good, send the pilot scoping doc.
[14:57] [15:10] Priya: ok wrapping up — i'll put the replay script, an example OTLP export, and a starter Optimize config in the repo. Jordan will send SOC2 and KMS appendix and pricing. Dana will push the sample prompts and any extra request IDs.
[15:22] Dana: thanks, this was super useful. appreciate how traceable the whole flow is.
[15:26] Jordan: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
